opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most practical ways to give people real control over video generation. Video is a much harder medium to iterate on than images. Generations take longer, they're more expensive, and if you're only working from a text prompt, you're rolling the dice on composition, character appearance, lighting, all of it at once. Images are fast and cheap to iterate on, and people already have a lot of intuition for how to edit them.

So the workflow we've seen work really well is to nail down the look first in the image domain. You generate a frame, maybe edit it a few times. Change the wardrobe, fix the background, adjust the color palette, until it's exactly what you want. Then you hand that to Veo as a starting frame or reference and say, "now bring this to life." The model can spend its capacity on motion, physics, and camera movement, instead of also having to invent the whole visual identity from scratch.

It also helps a lot with consistency, which is one of the biggest pain points for anyone trying to tell a story across multiple shots. If you have reference images for your character or your set, you can keep them stable from clip to clip in a way that's really hard to do with text alone. Language is just an underspecified way to describe what something looks like.

And more broadly, I think it reflects where these tools are heading. Image and video aren't really separate problems. A video model has to understand images deeply anyway, so letting people move fluidly between editing a still and animating it feels like the natural creative loop. It's much closer to how artists actually work: you sketch, you refine, and then you put things in motion.

r001.rationale: It describes generating and refining a frame in the image domain, then giving it to Veo as a starting frame or reference to create video.

r002.rationale: It says reference images for a character or set help keep them stable from clip to clip, guiding consistency across multiple shots.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing is that video is really hard to control. When you're generating a video, there are so many degrees of freedom. There's what's in the scene, how it's lit, how the camera moves, how things evolve over time. And if you try to specify all of that purely through text, you run into the limits of language pretty quickly. People aren't great at describing exactly what they want in words, and even when they are, the model has to interpret that description and might land somewhere different from what you had in mind.

Images are a much more precise way to communicate a lot of that intent. If I can give you a frame, I've already nailed down the composition, the characters, the style, the color palette, the mood. All of that is decided. And then the video model's job becomes much narrower. It's really about motion and time. How does this scene come to life? That's a much more tractable problem, and it's also a much more natural creative workflow. If you look at how people actually make films or animation, they storyboard. They sketch keyframes. They think in terms of still images first and then figure out how to connect them.

So what we're doing with image generation and editing in the Veo context is sort of borrowing that workflow. You can generate an image, iterate on it with editing tools until it's exactly right, and iteration on a still image is fast and cheap compared to iterating on video. Then you use that as the anchor for the video. And you can extend that to multiple frames, a first frame and a last frame, or reference images for a character or an object you want to stay consistent across shots.

And consistency is really where this pays off. One of the hardest problems in video generation is keeping a character looking like the same person across different clips, or keeping a product looking like the actual product. Images give you a way to pin that down that's much more reliable than hoping the text prompt gets you there every time.

The other thing I'd say is that it changes the relationship between the user and the model. Instead of a slot machine where you type something and hope, it becomes more of a conversation. You're making decisions at each stage, and the model is filling in the parts that would be tedious or impossible for a person to specify by hand. I think that's the direction these tools need to go if they're going to be useful for real creative work rather than just demos.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating and editing still images as a storyboard or keyframe workflow, then using them to anchor Veo video creation.

r002.rationale: It says edited images and reference images can pin down character or product appearance across shots, supporting consistency in multi-shot sequences.

astra-6.text:
I think the big value is control. With video, you’re asking for both what the scene looks like and how it evolves over time, and it can be hard to specify all of that in text. An image gives you a concrete starting point: the composition, the subject, the lighting, the visual style.

So you can use image generation and editing to iterate on that starting point, get it looking the way you want, and then use it to guide the video. That lets you focus the video prompt more on motion—what the subject does, how the camera moves, how the scene develops. It makes the creative process more iterative, because you can work out the appearance before you’re also trying to work out the movement.

r001.rationale: The response describes refining an image as a starting point to guide video creation, but does not identify image generation as a way to storyboard videos before creating them in Veo.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention consistency from image editing or using it to guide multi-shot sequences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big value is control. With video, you’re trying to specify both what the scene looks like and how it evolves over time, and doing all of that through text can be difficult. An image gives you a much more concrete starting point. You can work out the composition, the character, the lighting, and then use that as a reference for the video.

Image editing makes that process more iterative. You can say, “I like this scene, but let’s change the background or move this object,” and get the visual setup where you want it before introducing motion. Then, with Veo, you can focus on what happens next—how the subject moves, how the camera moves. That makes it easier to express your intent and build toward the result you have in mind.
